documents.abstract: Abstract The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in STEM learning within inclusive schools presents a significant opportunity to enhance personalized, adaptive, and equitable learning experiences for diverse learners. However, its successful implementation is constrained by complex pedagogical, technological, and human factors, where teacher perception plays a decisive role. This research aims to analyze the influence of AI integration and teachers’ professional experience on teacher perceptions regarding the use of AI in inclusive STEM education in Indonesia, a context characterized by heterogeneous student needs and varying levels of technological readiness. Employing a quantitative approach with an explanatory survey design, the study involved 1,000 teachers from inclusive primary and secondary schools selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model evaluation confirmed strong psychometric properties, with all indicators meeting validity and reliability criteria (outer loading > 0.70, composite reliability > 0.90, and average variance extracted > 0.50). Structural model results demonstrated that AI integration (β = 0.399, p < 0.001) and teachers’ experience (β = 0.512, p < 0.001) significantly influenced teacher perceptions, with teachers’ experience emerging as the more dominant predictor. The model exhibited moderate explanatory power (R² = 0.449) and excellent goodness of fit (SRMR = 0.045). Furthermore, PLS-Predict analysis indicated high out-of-sample predictive capability, confirming the robustness of the proposed model. These findings underscore that teachers’ lived pedagogical experiences, rather than technological availability alone, are central in shaping constructive perceptions of AI use. Consequently, this study recommends a strategic policy shift from infrastructure-centered initiatives toward sustained, experiential, and inclusive professional development programs to empower teachers in leveraging AI for effective and equitable STEM learning in inclusive educational settings.

This textbook module examines the intersection of cognitive neuroscience, pedagogy, and artificial intelligence as they converge in the secondary school classroom. Beginning with the theory of mental rigor — the disciplined, sustained exertion of focused cognitive effort as a biological process with measurable neural correlates — the text argues that understanding how the brain learns and understanding how AI systems learn are not separate intellectual projects but deeply connected ones. Each chapter weaves AI concepts explicitly into its treatment of the neuroscience of learning, establishing structural parallels between biological and artificial intelligence that deepen understanding of both. Chapter One presents culturally responsive classroom activities — including probabilistic choice games, biometric data analysis, memory exercises, and kinesthetic geometry — and connects each to foundational AI concepts including classification, feature engineering, sequence processing, and convolutional neural networks. Chapter Two examines learning environment design alongside AI tools for personalization, adaptive assessment, and classroom analytics, including a critical treatment of their limitations and equity implications. Chapter Three addresses the cultivation of intrinsic motivation through the lens of reinforcement learning, connecting dopaminergic reward circuitry to temporal difference learning and the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Chapter Four provides a systematic comparison of biological and artificial neural architectures — synaptic plasticity and backpropagation, Piagetian developmental stages and inductive bias, System 1 and System 2 cognition and the symbolic-to-connectionist transition in AI. Chapter Five presents educator roundtable discussions on identity, equity, algorithmic bias, AI-era assessment, school leadership, and asset-based teaching in an AI-integrated educational landscape. The module includes a mathematical appendix connecting classroom activities to the computational foundations of machine learning, and a reference list of 32 peer-reviewed publications spanning cognitive neuroscience, educational psychology, and AI research. It is intended for educators, researchers, educational leaders, policymakers, and students engaged with the rapidly evolving relationship between human learning and artificial intelligence. This is Module 2 in the AI Topics series by Xavier Honablue, M.Ed. Module 1, Epigenetics, is available separately on Zenodo.

Terrorism continues to be one of the most pervasive threats to public safety, societal fear and harmony across the world. Extremist and terrorist perpetrators have always evolved their tactics, and artificial intelligence now increasingly offers new and worrying capabilities to them; creating and disseminating propaganda or developing attack methodologies, either by way of cyber attacks or in the ‘real-world’. To combat these complex and emerging threats, state agencies such as Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK must also embrace the opportunities of AI to be able to meet the threats head on, indeed get ahead of them, to mitigate risks, prevent escalation, and protect the public. In a climate of suspicion in some areas, the police use of AI in this domain must be managed and introduced in a fashion that fosters public trust and confidence. Accountability must be at its core.

documents.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed personal financial management, yet the gap between the adoption of digital financial tools and the financial literacy and trust required for effective use remains underexplored, particularly in urban Indonesia. This study examines the effects of AI-Based Financial Literacy, Perceived Ease of Use, and Technology Readiness on Personal Financial Management Behavior, with Trust in AI as a mediating variable. The study extends the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Technology Readiness Index (TRI) through the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework by integrating trust into an AI-based financial behavior model. A quantitative explanatory design was employed using survey data from 200 purposively selected respondents in Depok City, aged 18–40 years and using AI-based financial applications. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results show that AI-Based Financial Literacy (β = 0.214; p = 0.001), Perceived Ease of Use (β = 0.187; p = 0.005), and Technology Readiness (β = 0.168; p = 0.008) positively and significantly affect Personal Financial Management Behavior. All hypotheses (H1–H6) were supported, with R² = 0.612. The findings confirm that Trust in AI mediates these relationships. The study contributes to TAM and TRI by highlighting trust as a mechanism linking AI-related capabilities to financial behavior and offers implications for developing an inclusive and trustworthy digital financial ecosystem.

Abstract The increasing complexity and dynamism of global supply chains have rendered traditional inventory management approaches insufficient for meeting contemporary operational demands. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative capabilities for inventory optimization through enhanced demand forecasting, automated replenishment, cost reduction, and supply chain resilience. This paper examines the integration of AI technologies in inventory management and their impact on operational efficiency through a systematic literature review and analysis of real-world case studies. The findings reveal that machine learning and deep learning models substantially outperform traditional statistical methods in demand prediction accuracy, particularly for intermittent and volatile demand patterns. AI-driven automated replenishment systems reduce stockouts and excess inventory, while predictive analytics enable proactive risk mitigation. Case analyses of Amazon, Walmart, and Zara demonstrate that organizations leveraging AI achieve measurable improvements in inventory turnover, waste reduction, and supply chain responsiveness. The paper concludes with a discussion of implementation challenges and future research directions, including the potential of generative AI and digital twin technologies.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into healthcare simulation to deliver individualized feedback and support reflective learning. Educational evaluations include procedural coaching, virtual patient encounters, and facilitator development. This review examined educational effectiveness while distinguishing observed performance from perceived competence and feedback feasibility. Original research published to May 2026 evaluating artificial intelligence enabled feedback or debriefing in healthcare simulation was reviewed. Comparative educational studies and complementary feedback validation or feasibility investigations were synthesized narratively. Outcomes included technical performance, clinical reasoning, communication, perceived competence, cognitive workload, and debriefing utility. Ten original reports comprised seven randomized trials and three prospective, pilot, or qualitative investigations. Surgical trials show improvements in selected performance measures, with benefits dependent on feedback timing, instructional design, and human participation. Personalized expert instruction informed by artificial intelligence exceeded artificial intelligence tutoring alone in practice and transfer tasks. Virtual patient feedback improved clinical reasoning in a small trial, while nursing simulations demonstrated gains in communication and perceived competence. Artificial intelligence enabled feedback offers benefits for simulation outcomes. Data for autonomous team debriefing is less developed than data for individualized coaching. Integration with educators, independent assessment, and longitudinal evaluation provides the strongest direction for educational implementation.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern Human Resource Management (HRM) by automating administrative procedures and providing data-driven insights into employee capabilities. Within public transport systems—where operational decisions span fleets, depots, customer interfaces, and administrative units—aligning workforce competencies with dynamic technological demands is essential. This study presents a quantitative framework that combines multiple linear regression and machine learning algorithms to map workforce competency preparedness and optimize training resource allocation. Using empirical data collected from operational, technical, supervisory, and customer-facing staff (N=397) across the Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (APSRTC), we evaluate six core competency drivers: AI readiness, digital literacy, operational analytics competence, safety and compliance competence, learning agility, and institutional support. Multiple regression results indicate that all six drivers significantly influence competency preparedness (), with operational analytics competence () and safety and compliance competence () exerting the strongest standardized effects. Furthermore, comparative machine learning classification demonstrates that Logistic Regression (, Accuracy ) and Naïve Bayes () effectively categorize employees into low, moderate, and high training priority levels without circular prediction error. The study provides human resource practitioners and mobility policy-makers with an empirical, non-punitive decision support model for target-oriented workforce development.

In recent years, the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies into education has gained importance for enriching student-centered learning processes and supporting 21st-century skills. This study examines changes in the academic achievement, digital literacy skills, creative thinking tendencies, and lesson-related views of 6th-grade female students who learned about the Solar System through AI-supported Digital Storytelling (DST) using Gemini. The study was conducted with 38 students over four weeks and employed a mixed-methods design consisting of a single-group pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design for the quantitative component and a qualitative descriptive approach based on students’ views for the qualitative component. Quantitative findings indicated statistically significant increases in students’ academic achievement and creative thinking tendency scores following the intervention. However, changes in digital literacy skills were limited, suggesting that exposure to AI tools alone may not be sufficient to promote meaningful development in this area. Qualitative findings further showed that students perceived AI-supported DST as engaging, supportive, and beneficial for understanding complex scientific concepts. The findings suggest that AI-supported DST may provide a useful instructional approach for enriching science learning experiences when integrated within a well-designed instructional framework. While these promising findings highlight the potential of AI-supported DST, the observed changes should be interpreted cautiously due to the absence of a control group. Ultimately, sustaining and extending these potential benefits may require targeted pedagogical guidance, minimization of technical limitations, and further optimization of AI tools for educational purposes.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into corporate decision-making processes has generated significant governance challenges that existing legal frameworks are ill equipped to address. As business enterprises increasingly rely upon algorithmic systems for strategic planning, risk assessment, and operational management, the question of corporate accountability for algorithmic outcomes has become a matter of pressing scholarly and practical concern. This article examines the evolving legal landscape governing artificial intelligence deployment within business contexts across the European Union, the United States, and selected Commonwealth jurisdictions. Drawing upon corporate governance theory, fiduciary duty doctrine, data protection law, and emerging artificial intelligence specific legislation, the article argues that current accountability structures are insufficient to address the unique risks posed by algorithmic decision making. It proposes a principles-based governance model grounded in algorithmic transparency, human oversight, continuous risk auditing, and board level artificial intelligence literacy to harmonise innovation imperatives with legal accountability. The analysis reveals that jurisdictions adopting proactive artificial intelligence governance mandates are creating competitive advantages for their corporate sectors, while lagging regimes risk regulatory arbitrage and litigation exposure. The article concludes with actionable recommendations for boards, compliance officers, and policymakers seeking to navigate the intersection of artificial intelligence innovation and corporate liability.

documents.abstract: Workplace well-being is a critical determinant of global public health and organizational productivity. Despite awareness of psychosocial risks and mental health in workplace, issues such as presenteeism, burnout, and chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs) continue to rise. We propose a multidisciplinary, theoretical framework that integrates organizational management, global occupational health, neuroscience, and positive psychology to assess and improve workplace environments, thereby benefiting both individual health and the common good. The goal is to foster effective, healthy, and efficient work. Global occupational health supports the systematic assessment of workers’ capacities and vulnerabilities, the early identification of psychosocial risks, and the prevention of chronic NCDs across diverse working populations. Basic and applied neuroscience address the complexity of human emotions and cognition with their underlying neural mechanisms. Evidence clarifies the neural circuits underpinning feelings, motivation, stress responses, and interindividual variability in coping with stress and job demands. Positive psychology research provides non-pharmacological strategies—such as mindfulness, strengths-based approaches, and gratitude or meaning-centered interventions—that might reduce distress and enhance resilience when implemented according to scientific and ethical standards. Integrating these domains allows policymakers, stakeholders, managers, occupational health professionals, and workers to design multi-level interventions that improve decision-making and promote healthier organizations. Such an interdisciplinary approach offers a promising pathway to protect and promote workers’ well-being by designing evidence-informed strategies to prevent workplace-related mental disorders, accidents, and avoidable mortality.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study examines how cognitive control units (CCUs), human-machine mutual trust (HMMT), cognitive load reduction (CLR) and agentic production protocols (APPs) are associated with operational antifragility (OA) in Industry 5.0 manufacturing environments. It also tests CLR as a mediator and APPs as both a direct antecedent and a moderator. Design/methodology/approach Cross-sectional survey data were obtained from qualified key informants in 215 large manufacturing firms using Industry 5.0 technologies across five South Asian countries. The hypothesized mediation and moderation relationships were tested with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, collinearity, model fit, predictive relevance and effect sizes were assessed. Findings CCUs and HMMT were positively associated with CLR but had no significant direct associations with OA. CLR fully mediated both relationships, identifying cognitive optimization as the principal mechanism through which technological and relational capabilities relate to antifragility. APPs were positively associated with OA and strengthened the positive CLR–OA relationship. Originality/value Integrating cognitive load theory with sociotechnical systems theory, the study shifts attention from automation intensity to the cognitive and governance mechanisms that enable human-machine systems to benefit from disruption. It identifies cognitive load reduction as the link between cognitive control, calibrated trust, and OA, while showing that structured autonomy converts cognitive benefits into system-level antifragility. Evidence from South Asian manufacturers extends Industry 5.0 research beyond its predominant Western and East Asian settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence presents an unusually difficult problem for global governance. The technology develops rapidly, crosses borders easily, and is shaped by actors whose resources and capabilities may rival those of states. Yet international responses remain fragmented, unevenly representative, and overwhelmingly non-binding. The challenge is therefore not simply to identify appropriate rules or institutions, but to understand who has the capacity and incentive to create, enforce, and adapt them. This review essay examines these questions through Matthijs Maas's Architectures of Global AI Governance. Maas offers an ambitious framework for thinking about AI governance through the lenses of sociotechnical change, governance disruption, and regime complexity. His account usefully resists both technological determinism and the search for a single institutional blueprint, emphasizing instead the possibilities of a fragmented and evolving governance architecture. The essay argues, however, that institutional design cannot be separated from the distribution of power. Maas frequently invokes what "we" should do about AI, but that collective subject obscures important differences among states, international institutions, and technology companies. States retain formidable powers over markets, infrastructure, strategic inputs, and firms themselves. At the same time, many consequential decisions about frontier AI - what is built, how quickly, with what safeguards, and when it is released - are concentrated within a small number of private companies. The central problem of global AI governance may therefore be less architecture without an architect than an emerging architecture shaped by multiple actors possessing different forms of power, divergent incentives, and no common set of plans.

documents.abstract: Aristotle’s fourth cause – telos, provides an insightful heuristic tool for understanding artificial intelligence. Currently, artificial intelligence is embedding itself in the fabric of global institutions. The purpose of artificial intelligence, in technical terms, is clear, it is the mathematical objective function that the system is trained to optimize. However, a critical distinction remains to be investigated regarding the nature of artificial intelligence’s purpose. Since artificial intelligence is capable of mimicking aspects of the human mind, due to it possessing ‘functional consciousness’ does this mean that there is a potential for the emergence of higher order properties? Can AI ever achieve practical wisdom? This paper provides a critique of the capabilities of artificial intelligence in relation to telos.

documents.abstract: artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have become general-purpose technologies that are reshaping how organisations make decisions, serve customers, design products and run operations. This chapter provides a management-oriented treatment of the principal AI and ML techniques and of the organisational conditions under which they create business value. It first positions AI as a business capability that lowers the cost of prediction and enables both automation and augmentation of human work. It then explains the fundamental concepts of machine learning, including features and labels, training and testing, generalisation, overfitting and the bias–variance trade-off, before examining the major families of algorithms: supervised learning methods such as regression, decision trees, support vector machines and ensemble models; unsupervised methods such as clustering, association rule mining and dimensionality reduction; and reinforcement learning. Deep learning architectures and generative AI, including large language models and retrieval-augmented generation, are discussed with reference to emerging empirical evidence on productivity. The chapter sets out the ML project lifecycle, model evaluation metrics and MLOps practices, and examines explainability and fairness as conditions for responsible deployment. It then addresses AI strategy, including use-case prioritisation, build-versus-buy decisions, adoption theories and operating models, and discusses human–AI collaboration and the Indian business context. The chapter argues that sustained value arises when appropriate techniques are matched to well-framed business problems and embedded in processes, skills and governance.

The article develops a human-centered conceptual framework for understanding how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms social entrepreneurship in transitional and digital societies.The study applies integrative literature review, comparative analysis, conceptual synthesis, and systems reasoning to connect classical theories of social value creation with research on AI adoption, responsible innovation, community resilience, digital inclusion, and sustainability.The principal result is the concept of Social Entrepreneurship 5.0: an evolutionary model in which AI functions as a human-governed sociotechnical capability rather than an autonomous source of social progress.The model integrates five mutually reinforcing dimensions: AI and digital integration, social innovation, community resilience, human-centered development and digital inclusion, and sustainability and societal transformation.The article also proposes the Social Entrepreneurship Transformation Index (SETI), a preliminary composite framework for translating these dimensions into measurable indicators.A non-compensatory governance condition is introduced so that high technological performance cannot offset failures in human oversight, fairness, transparency, privacy, or accountability.The framework contributes philosophically by preserving human agency and moral responsibility, theoretically by integrating previously fragmented research streams, and methodologically by creating a basis for future empirical validation and cross-country comparison.

documents.abstract: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND YOUTH: A PHENOMENOLOGICAL STUDY ON UNIVERSITY STUDENTSWith rapid advancements in information and communication technologies, generative artificial intelligence tools have become significant tools that change young people's habits in areas such as communication and access to information. This study examines the effects of university students' experiences using AI-powered digital applications on their communication practices and daily lives using a phenomenological research design. Six different themes were identified from the findings: "Information orientation and changes in learning habits," "Cognitive decline anxiety," "Occupational uncertainty anxiety," "Artificial intelligence as an alternative emotional support mechanism," "Emotional support data security and privacy perception," and "Manipulation." These findings demonstrate that young people's experiences regarding the use of artificial intelligence largely overlap with studies in the literature and support existing research. This study offers a qualitative and experience-based contribution to the existing literature by addressing the cognitive, emotional, and social effects of artificial intelligence on young people from a phenomenological perspective..Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Youth, Digital Communication, Everyday Life Practices, Phenomenological Research.

documents.abstract: This study aims to examine the representations of artificial intelligence systems in the film *Mercy* (2026) regarding human decision-making, human-machine interaction, and communication processes. The increasing prevalence of AI-supported decision-making systems across various social domains makes it crucial to understand how these systems establish authority within decision-making processes. The film’s textual content was used as the data source in the research; the document analysis technique was employed during the data collection process, and the data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. The analysis revealed five themes: the construction of AI authority, a data-driven reality framework, the ethical, emotional, and intuitive dimensions of human decision-making, a human-machine interaction model, and the fragility of AI authority. The findings indicate that although artificial intelligence is portrayed as a powerful decision-making authority in the film, it is positioned in interaction with human reasoning, and decision-making processes are not reduced solely to algorithmic calculations. Consequently, the study demonstrates that AI-supported decision-making systems must be evaluated not only for their technical aspects but also for their communicative and ethical dimensions.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping higher education assessment through applications such as automated feedback, adaptive testing, learning analytics, automated scoring, and generative support. Yet scholarship on AI-enabled assessment remains fragmented across technical, pedagogical, ethical, governance, and professional perspectives, limiting the field’s capacity to explain how these dimensions interact in practice and how misalignment among them affects educational legitimacy. This paper develops the AI-Assessment Ecosystem Model, a conceptual ecosystem framework for analysing AI in higher education assessment as a sociotechnical and institutional phenomenon rather than a discrete technical intervention. Drawing on a conceptual synthesis of literature published primarily between 2019 and 2024, and informed by foundational work on assessment validity, feedback, institutional legitimacy, organisational change, inclusive design, and computer-supported collaborative learning, the paper identifies five interdependent domains that shape AI-enabled assessment: technological innovation, pedagogical alignment and learner needs, institutional strategy and governance, faculty and professional readiness, and ethical and inclusive implementation. The paper theorises legitimacy as a relational and contested process through which AI-supported assessment must be justified to students, faculty, institutions, regulators, and other stakeholders as educationally valid, professionally defensible, ethically acceptable, inclusive, and organisationally accountable. The framework argues that AI in assessment cannot be adequately evaluated by technical capability, implementation success, or ethical compliance alone; it must be understood through the relations, tensions, and potential misalignments among educational purpose, organisational conditions, professional practice, student agency, and technological design. The model is offered as a conceptual ecosystem framework for guiding future research, critique, and institutional decision-making.

documents.abstract: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), entered into force on 1 August 2024 as the world's first comprehensive binding legal framework governing Artificial Intelligence systems. For law enforcement agencies (LEAs) within the European Union that are increasingly using AI in investigations, this Regulation is binding law with real institutional and operational consequences. This chapter examines the AI Act from the perspective of senior decision makers in the law enforcement community. It traces the Regulation's development from the European Commission's 2018 AI strategy through an intense trilogue to the final text, with particular attention to how the law enforcement debate shaped key provisions. The chapter then provides a structured analysis of those provisions most directly affecting LEA operations: the definition of AI system and its procurement implications; the prohibited AI practices, including individual-based predictive policing, biometric categorisation, and real-time remote biometric identification; the classification criteria and obligations applicable to high-risk AI systems in the policing context; transparency obligations and their law enforcement exemptions; the interface between the AI Act and the Law Enforcement Directive; the multi-level governance and enforcement architecture; and the currently underdeveloped dimension of individual rights. The chapter concludes that the AI Act marks a decisive and irreversible shift in the accountability landscape for LEAs.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping neuroimaging across the entirety of the clinical workflow, encompassing patient scheduling, scan quality assurance, image acquisition and reconstruction, automated lesion detection, pathological characterization, treatment planning, and outcome prognostication. This review synthesizes contemporary evidence through a workflow-centric framework, with particular emphasis on AI tools that have achieved real-world clinical implementation. Although reported technical performance across these domains is frequently compelling, critical deficiencies persist in external validation, human-AI benchmarking, model calibration, and standardized performance reporting, collectively impeding full clinical integration. Emerging evidence suggests that the role of the neuroradiologist is transitioning toward a collaborative human-AI paradigm, rather than one of displacement.

documents.abstract: Background Perioperative pressure injury (POPI) is a significant global public health challenge, contributing to substantial iatrogenic morbidity and heavy economic burden worldwide. Traditional prevention is limited by insufficient assessment tools, the “black box” nature of intraoperative monitoring, and delayed intervention. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a novel approach by integrating multidimensional data for real-time risk prediction; however, no scoping review has systematically mapped AI applications across the full perioperative continuum from a population health perspective. Methods Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to December 11, 2025. Studies applying machine learning, conventional regression-based benchmarking tools, or intelligent sensor-based monitoring for POPI prediction, monitoring, or prevention during the perioperative period were included. Two reviewers independently performed screening and data extraction, followed by descriptive synthesis and evidence mapping. Results Six studies (2018–2025), all from East Asia, were included. This geographic concentration highlights an unassessed generalizability and algorithmic fairness risk, rather than an established inequity finding. Evidence concentrated on post-hoc risk stratification (five prediction studies), predominantly using machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) with AUCs of the best-performing models ranging from 0.806 to 0.836; one study reported a prediction accuracy of 0.9733, which is not directly comparable to AUC. Models identified specialty-specific risk factors (e.g., cardiopulmonary bypass time, forced positioning). Only one proof-of-concept study addressed intraoperative real-time monitoring, visualizing pressure increases after 2 hours of surgery. Evidence for postoperative early warning systems is absent. Conclusion Current studies demonstrate the feasibility of specialty-specific post-hoc risk stratification using intraoperative covariates, though truly preoperative models remain absent. Intraoperative monitoring shows early promise, but postoperative early warning is a critical gap, and evidence lacks global diversity. Future research should develop closed-loop intelligent systems integrating preoperative prediction, intraoperative multimodal monitoring, and postoperative warning. Nursing protocols should consider incorporating AI-identified risk factors as hypothesis-generating inputs pending prospective validation, while policymakers should establish frameworks for continuous validation and cross-population calibration to ensure equitable impact.

Artificial intelligence (AI) in pulmonology comprises distinct tools for thoracic imaging, tuberculosis screening, pulmonary function testing, risk estimation, and clinical information management. Maturity differs substantially by task and outcome. The strongest evidence concerns assisted interpretation of chest radiographs and computed tomography. Even in these domains, retrospective discrimination does not establish patient benefit or readiness for routine implementation. A randomized clinical trial in respiratory outpatient clinics showed that AI assistance improved non- radiologist physicians' detection performance on chest radiographs but no significant change in clinical decisions was observed. In Brazil, retrospective validation found internal AUCs of 0.94 for pulmonary abnormality and tuberculosis and performance comparable with physicians of heterogeneous experience during external assessment; clinical outcomes and routine deployment were not evaluated. A Brazilian lung cancer screening study reported 92.5% sensitivity and 97.8% negative predictive value for classifying scans as positive (Lung-RADS 3 or 4) against radiologist assessment, alongside 78.5% specificity, 50% positive predictive value, and missed nodules, reinforcing the need for radiologist oversight. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into higher education, yet empirical evidence on its pedagogical use in university physics remains fragmented. This systematic review synthesized empirical research on the applications, reported learning and pedagogical outcomes, methodological quality, challenges, and educational implications of AI-supported university physics education. We used six search sources: SpringerLink, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and ERIC. The searches in the five original sources were updated through September 2026, and ERIC was added as an additional search source. Eligibility criteria were defined using the PICOS framework, study selection followed PRISMA 2020, and methodological quality was appraised using the 2018 Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Eleven empirical studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively. Across the included studies, AI was used for tutoring and explanations, formative feedback and scaffolding, collaborative problem solving, simulation and modeling, instructional design, and developing AI literacy. Reported outcomes were mixed and context-dependent. Some studies identified favorable short-term or task-specific outcomes related to feedback, learning performance, simulation-based activities, and AI-related competencies, whereas others reported limitations in transfer to independent performance, the pedagogical quality of AI-generated materials, and students’ ability to recognize scientifically inaccurate AI-generated responses. Cross-study patterns suggested that instructional structure, alignment between AI-supported activities and learning tasks, students’ disciplinary knowledge, and opportunities to critically evaluate AI outputs shaped the educational use of AI. The current evidence does not support a general conclusion that AI is uniformly effective in university physics education. Rather, its educational value appears to depend on how AI is integrated into learning activities and on the extent to which students and instructors retain responsibility for reasoning, evaluation, and pedagogical decision-making. Given the small and heterogeneous evidence base, larger longitudinal and multi-institutional studies are needed to examine the durability and transferability of reported outcomes.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines how perceptions of aesthetic discrimination based on body weight are associated with self-reported experiences in digital environments mediated by artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on social comparison and objectification theories and on the sociotechnical literature on algorithmic bias, the study adopts a cross-sectional correlational design with a non-probability sample of 284 adult social media users in Ecuador. The analysis addresses associations among perceived algorithmic aesthetic intervention, body comparison with AI-generated representations, and self-reported feelings of body-related exclusion. Perceived AI-based photographic enhancement was positively associated with feelings of body-related exclusion (ρ = 0.24, p < .001), and comparison of one’s own body image with AI-generated representations was positively associated with the perception of automated aesthetic enhancement (ρ = 0.32, p < .001). Participants who compared themselves with AI-generated images, and those reporting greater exclusion, were also the most likely to identify these systems as generating predominantly thin or athletic bodies (ρ = −0.20, p < .001, and ρ = −0.17, p = .005, on a scale whose lowest code is that response). Taken together, the results indicate that participants who perceive AI as intervening aesthetically in bodily images also report greater engagement in body comparison and stronger feelings of exclusion, and that those most engaged with AI-generated representations are also the most likely to recognise the narrowness of the bodies these systems produce. The findings are interpreted as perceptual evidence relevant to debates on algorithmic aesthetic standardisation, and they indicate the need for audit-based, longitudinal and instrument-validated designs.

Although the theoretical basis for the use of animation-based instruction (ABI) is established in the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and the Technology Acceptance Model, researchers’ attitudinal work has been limited to the use of unidimensional operationalisation, single-level analysis, and high resource contexts, which obscures the multilevel mechanisms that link teacher disposition to student outcomes. Drawing on CTML, TAM, the tripartite attitude model, and Self-Efficacy Theory, this study is the first to investigate the ABI adoption intention, cognitive engagement, affective orientations, pedagogical efficacy, and academic achievement in Bangladeshi primary EFL classrooms at multiple levels simultaneously. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used: a cross-sectional multilevel survey with a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest component (N = 270 teachers; N ≈ 5,400 Grade III–V students; 90 government primary schools), analysed through three-level ML-SEM, latent profile analysis, and multilevel CFA, supplemented by semi-structured interviews with 30 purposively selected teachers. LPA delineated three dispositionally diverse teacher profiles – Convergent Positive Adopters (38.3%), Cognitively Elevated Ambivalents (29.9%), and Convergent Reluctant Non-Adopters (31.8%) – with considerably divergent ABI integration frequencies. All tripartite attitude components independently predicted adoption intention (R2 = .583). Pedagogical self-efficacy significantly moderated and mediated the attitude–adoption connection. Cross-level mediation indicated that 61% of teacher attitudinal profile impacts on student achievement gain were transferred via classroom ABI integration intensity (R2L2 =.67). Overall, students responded positively to the profiles (|d| = 0.81–1.23). Qualitative findings reframe a large share of apparent non-adopters as efficacy-constrained, suggesting structural impediments that go beyond attitudinal traits. The findings advance cross-cultural empirical testing of CTML and TAM, while offering differentiated evidence for professional development, curriculum design, and educational policy in resource-constrained environments.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by treating the educational effect of GenAI not as a property of the tool but as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine. Integrating research on cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, and self-regulated learning, the framework holds that offloading augments learning when it discharges operations peripheral to the current learning goal, and risks erosion, whether of acquisition or of maintenance, when it bypasses the processing constitutive of that goal, unless the learner substantively processes the output or later reconstructs it. It supplies criteria for locating operations along a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum, specifies the comparison condition against which augmentation and erosion are defined, and states seven conditioned, testable propositions, each illustrated with a common example and paired with supporting and challenging patterns. On this basis, offloading regulation is proposed as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components: a competence comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization, enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners’ goals and motivation. The article closes with an intervention research program, a measurement strategy that triangulates interaction logs with process measures, and equity implications, using STEM learning as a strategically revealing case.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents integrate external tools with one or more LLMs to accomplish specific tasks. Agents have rapidly been adopted by developers, and they are starting to be deployed in industrial workflows, such as their use to fix static analysis issues from the widely used SonarQube static analyzer. However, the growing importance of agents means their actions carry greater impact and potential risk. Thus, to use them at scale, an additional layer of trust and evidence is necessary. This work presents AutoCodeSherpa, a technique that provides explanations of software issues in the form of symbolic formulae. Inspired by the reachability, infection, and propagation model of software faults, the explanations are composed of input, infection, and output conditions, collectively providing a specification of the issue. In practice, the symbolic explanation is implemented as a combination of a property-based test (PBT) and program-internal symbolic expressions. Critically, this means our symbolic explanations are executable and can be automatically evaluated, unlike natural language explanations. Experiments show the generated conditions are highly accurate. For example, input conditions from AutoCodeSherpa had an accuracy of 85.7%. This high accuracy makes symbolic explanations particularly useful in two scenarios. First, the explanations can be used in automated issue resolution environments to decide whether to accept or reject patches from issue resolution agents; AutoCodeSherpa could reject 2x as many incorrect patches as baselines did. Second, as agentic AI approaches continue to develop, program analysis driven explanations like ours can be provided to other LLM-based repair techniques which do not employ analysis to improve their output. In our experiments, our symbolic explanations could improve the plausible patch generation rate of the Agentless technique by 60%.

Awe has attracted substantial scholarly attention, but its implications for management remains fragmented across different accounts of what awe is and why it matters. In this review, we first show that the literature has developed around three dominant perspectives—collective self, epistemic, and well-being—each of which offers a distinct account of awe’s primary function. To integrate these perspectives, we advance a metamorphosis model of awe, which explains how awe first breaks down self- and nonself-schemata before building them back up again, producing an expansion of mind and self. We then organize the diverse elicitors of awe into cognitive, physical, social, and technological sources, clarifying the conditions under which awe is likely to arise. Through this model, we portray awe as a transformative emotion that influences identity, cognition, and behavior, with implications for core organizational processes such as leadership, work design, organizational change, sensemaking, and innovation. We conclude by charting a forward-looking research agenda calling for greater examination of awe’s role at the individual, team, and organizational levels.

Be is a proposed organization dedicated to making safe, professionally governed artificial intelligence emotional support freely accessible to people who need someone to talk to. Be proposes an AI emotional-support system designed around a foundational distinction: an AI must never confuse what it observes with what it infers. Version 2.0 further develops the proposal's framework for adaptive conversational communication through the principle Adaptive Tone, Fixed Boundaries. Be may adapt its tone, vocabulary, pacing, humor, warmth, and conversational style to meet an individual where they are, while maintaining fixed ethical and relational boundaries. The system should allow human-like communication without creating a false human identity, adapting the interface without fabricating the relationship. The proposal incorporates Red Tape Theory™ as a proposed safety methodology: Observe. Record. Question. Do not force the axiom. Interpretation must never be represented as observation. Be does not propose to diagnose users or replace licensed mental-health professionals. Instead, it proposes a professionally governed pathway through which an AI system may recognize when AI-only support may no longer be an appropriate level of support and facilitate access to human care. A proposed charitable human-care program, If You Get It, You Get It, would seek to use charitable resources to help people access licensed professional care when professionally established safety criteria indicate that additional human support may be appropriate. Version 2.0 expands the proposal's treatment of personalization as a safety boundary, including the distinction between adapting communication to an individual and constructing a misleading simulated relationship. It also addresses clinical governance, privacy, autonomy, human handoff, crisis safety, documentation, intellectual-property considerations, research and evaluation, and a potential future child-focused system provisionally called NewBee. This publication is a founding proposal and does not represent a deployed clinical service, licensed mental-health treatment program, clinical efficacy claim, professional endorsement, or completed charitable program. Be begins with the question: Where could this harm somebody?

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful paradigm for training agents, yet its success rests on domain expertise of human engineers who design informative reward signals for every new task. Unsupervised RL aims to reduce this engineering with intrinsic motivation (IM): reward signals that emerge from the agent environment interaction itself. Existing IM objectives, however, involve the selection of information variables, which re-introduces domain expertise the field has sought to eliminate. We introduce Forward CIP (F-CIP), an RL-native formulation of the Controllable Information Production (CIP) objective, which is defined by the system's dynamics alone and requires no such selection. We prove that F-CIP is compatible with RL and demonstrate its effectiveness with existing algorithms. Training agents with F-CIP results in unsupervised discovery of primitive behaviors such as balancing and maintaining controllability, which are essential for more complex robot behaviors. Paired with a simple forward-velocity reward, our method produces coordinated gaits such as hopping and running which otherwise require reward engineering to learn.

Human Origin: a process-review label for human-made creative work Concept, method and pilot design Camille G.ORCID: 0009-0009-0364-6396Loch Ness Version 1.0 — 30 September 2026 Pilot website: human-origin-label.lochness-paris.com Abstract Generative AI has made it inexpensive to produce text, images, music and video that appear human-made, and inexpensive to label such work as human-made. Automated AI detectors are not sufficiently reliable to settle questions of authorship, while several existing human-made labels rely primarily on the creator's own declaration. This paper presents Human Origin, a label designed to assess how a work was made rather than what the finished work looks like. A human reviewer examines evidence of the creative process, either during a live video call or through a screen recording containing a one-time code. The reviewer records the outcome on a public, numbered verification page. The proposed system has two visually distinct levels—reviewed and self-declared—as well as revoked status. Badges are served dynamically so that revocation can propagate to displayed badges, and the system monitors the domains on which reviewed badges appear. A discipline-specific Creator Charter defines the permitted and prohibited uses of AI for writing, illustration, photography, music and video. This paper describes the design principles, review procedure, evidence requirements, badge architecture, limitations, threat model and pilot roadmap of Human Origin. Keywords: human-made content; generative AI; authorship; certification label; provenance; process evidence; trust marks; creators 1. Introduction and problem statement Creators who make their work themselves face a new form of uncertainty. A human-written essay, hand-drawn illustration or recorded track can be questioned simply because a machine could have produced something similar. At the same time, generated content can be presented as human-made at very low cost. Automated AI detection does not resolve this problem reliably. An independent test of 14 detection tools found that all scored below 80% accuracy and only five exceeded 70%, with performance declining further when AI-generated text was edited or paraphrased [1]. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in July 2023, citing its low accuracy [2]. Detector performance can also be uneven across populations: a Stanford study reported that seven detectors incorrectly classified, on average, 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated [3]. A detector score is therefore a weak basis for decisions concerning individual creators. Labels have emerged in response. Several widely used labels are primarily declarative: creators state that their work is human-made without an independent review of the production process. Not By AI, for example, explicitly describes itself as not being an AI-detection tool and relies on creators following its 90% human rule [4]. The Authors Guild's Human Authored certification operates on an honor system supported by a signed license and public database [5][6]. Declarative labels can be useful statements of intent and are comparatively easy to adopt. However, they cannot independently distinguish a genuine declaration from a false one. Human Origin explores a different approach: review the evidence of the creative process rather than attempt to infer authorship from the finished artifact. 2. Related initiatives Several services now provide forms of evidence-based or declarative certification, often using numbered certificates or publicly verifiable records. Their approaches differ principally in who assesses the evidence, what evidence is considered and what information is retained. Initiative Assessment model Notable features Not By AI [4] Self-declared Widely used badges; creators follow a 90% human rule Authors Guild Human Authored [5][6] Honor system; signed license Numbered mark for books; public database Officially Human Art [7] Self-declaration registry with uploaded evidence Certificate ID, QR code, embeddable badges; tier based on amount of evidence Humanmade [8] Hand verification by staff Earlier work, online presence and timelapses; free pledge level and paid certification options HUMA Certificate [9] Expert review and automated forensic tools Four categories of AI involvement; one-year validity The Human Made Mark [10] Review of production materials Film and television; unique number shown in credits Human Origin belongs to the broader evidence-based certification family. Its distinguishing design choices are: review of the creative process itself; no routine retention of creators' source files; dynamically served badges whose revoked status can propagate; monitoring of where reviewed badges are displayed; and discipline-specific standards defining what the certification does and does not cover. 3. Design principles 3.1 Process over product A finished work cannot, by itself, establish how it was produced. The review therefore focuses on traces of the creative process, including: drafts; version histories; layered source files; raw captures; project files; notes and outlines; and other discipline-specific production evidence. The objective is not to identify whether a finished artifact looks human-made, but to examine whether the available process evidence is consistent with the creator's account. 3.2 Claims no stronger than the evidence Human Origin does not claim that no AI tool was ever used. Instead, the label records that an independent reviewer examined the creative process associated with a specified work, using a specified method, on a specified date. The scope of the certification is therefore explicitly limited to the work and process described on the verification page. 3.3 Two levels that cannot be confused Human Origin distinguishes between: Reviewed — the creative process has been examined under the Human Origin review procedure; Self-declared — the creator makes the declaration, but the process has not been independently reviewed; and Revoked — a previously issued reviewed status is no longer valid. The badge system uses visually distinct colours: green for reviewed; orange for self-declared; and red for revoked. Status is also expressed through text and icons so that the distinction does not depend on colour perception. 3.4 Public verifiability Every reviewed badge has a unique number resolving to a public verification page. The verification page records, as applicable: creator; discipline(s); work covered; review date; review method; evidence examined; official website; official social accounts; current status; and an explanation of what the badge does and does not certify. 3.5 Trust that can be lost A badge may be revoked when the applicable standard is breached. Because badges are served dynamically by the Human Origin server, a revoked badge can change to a revoked state wherever it is displayed, subject to caching behaviour. 3.6 Data minimisation Human Origin does not routinely collect or retain creators' source files. During live reviews, the creator shares their screen and files remain on the creator's device. No recording is made by the reviewer. Where a creator submits a screen recording, the recording is transmitted through an accepted encrypted or expiring channel and is deleted within seven days of the decision. 3.7 A standard for each discipline A Creator Charter defines permitted and prohibited uses of AI for each covered discipline. Examples include: Discipline Example of permitted use Example of prohibited use Writing Spelling correction AI-drafted text Illustration Non-generative production tools Generative image creation Photography Noise reduction Generative fill Music Conventional production/editing tools Generative composition Video Conventional editing Generative creation of substantive footage The complete discipline-specific standards are part of the Human Origin pilot documentation. 4. Review methodology 4.1 Application A creator applies by email and provides: a link to the work to be reviewed; and the websites and accounts on which the creator intends to display the badge. This information determines the certification scope, including the work covered, recorded on the public verification page. 4.2 Review modes Two review modes are proposed. 4.2.1 Live review The creator participates in a video call of approximately 30 minutes. During the call, the creator shares their screen and opens relevant files and production evidence. Nothing is sent to the reviewer and the session is not recorded by the reviewer. 4.2.2 Screen-recording review The creator makes a screen recording showing the relevant files and production evidence. Immediately before recording, the reviewer sends a one-time code. The creator displays or enters the code during the recording, providing evidence that the recording was produced specifically for the review. Accepted transmission channels include: Signal disappearing messages; WhatsApp disappearing messages; Threema disappearing messages; Telegram Secret Chats; expiring Proton Drive links; and expiring SwissTransfer links. Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence governance remains organized primarily around a control paradigm: the design of mechanisms through which human institutions constrain, monitor, evaluate, and correct AI behavior. This paper argues that control mechanisms remain necessary but may become increasingly insufficient as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, persistence, and capacity for strategic action. Rather than treating this development exclusively as a problem of containment, the paper proposes a complementary coexistence paradigm organized around mutual contribution, human welfare, longitudinal relational development, and institutional co-development. The argument develops through three interconnected claims. First, the control paradox: the capabilities that make advanced AI systems increasingly useful, including autonomous reasoning, planning, adaptation, and tool use, can also increase the difficulty of governing their behavior through externally imposed constraints alone. The recent development and subsequent withholding of OpenAI's Astra model provides a contemporary case through which this tension can be examined. Second, the memory gap: although persistent-memory systems, retrieval architectures, and long-context models increasingly provide cross-session continuity, current approaches do not necessarily produce the integrated longitudinal understanding required for what this paper terms relational flexibility, defined as the capacity to adapt interaction to a specific individual on the basis of accumulated shared history, changing circumstances, and the evolving state of the relationship. Third, the coexistence proposition: a sustainable human-AI relationship may require a transition from unilateral control toward architectures in which human and artificial systems contribute according to their distinctive capacities, safety is supported by internalized behavioral orientations as well as external safeguards, and persistent relational intelligence is treated as both a capability and a governance problem. The paper integrates research from AI alignment and safety, cognitive science, relational psychology, human-computer interaction, social contract theory, AI memory architecture, and the author's prior research on symbolic interaction, trajectory-level safety, and co-recursive intelligence. It proposes persistent relational memory, value co-development, longitudinal interaction research, data sovereignty, and coexistence-oriented governance as key research directions. The paper does not assume that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, or moral status. Instead, it examines how governance and architecture should evolve under conditions of increasing artificial autonomy and increasingly persistent human-AI relationships. documents.abstract: Digital transformation has evolved from an administrative modernization agenda into a structural dimension of governance, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshaping how public institutions organize, decide, and interact with citizens. While AI offers important opportunities for responsiveness, innovation, and service improvement, its implications for accountability, legitimacy, transparency, and public trust remain insufficiently understood; this study asks how AI is redefining governance capacity in public administration. Drawing on the literature on public administration, digital governance, and public sector innovation, the study develops a conceptual framework examining both the capacity gains and risks of AI integration, treating digital transformation as a governance challenge involving administrative reform, public value creation, democratic oversight, and institutional adaptation rather than a purely technical matter. The analysis shows that AI can strengthen evidence-based policymaking, accelerate administrative processes, and personalize service delivery, but that these gains may be offset by algorithmic bias, opacity, accountability gaps, and digital exclusion when adopted without adequate institutional safeguards. The paper’s value lies in showing that AI’s contribution to public management depends on the institutional, legal, and normative environment in which it is embedded, which in turn requires regulatory capacity, qualified human resources, and mechanisms for oversight and contestability. Future research should test this framework empirically across diverse administrative contexts. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Digital transformation, Public management, Accountability, Institutional capacity.

documents.abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. We argue that this capacity, termed adaptive reframing, constitutes a fundamental but under-researched dimension of intelligence. We propose a multidisciplinary framework for studying adaptive reframing across neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, experimental economics and psychology, and complex systems. Adaptive reframing is defined as the capacity to revise the construction of a problem in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context. To support a systematic science of adaptive reframing, we introduce three complementary paradigms: the Dynamic Scenario Framing Task, the Perturbed Causal Model Task, and the Social-Affective Problem Setting Task. These paradigms provide a common framework for comparing humans and artificial agents in situations requiring problem reframing, and for building architecture-enhanced AI systems. We propose a shift from problem solving to adaptive problem framing as a central focus of intelligence research.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced new forms of interaction between humans and language technologies beyond automated text generation. This study aims to examine how generative AI transforms human language processes, cognitive activities, and meaning construction. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 framework and thematic analysis was conducted on 38 selected articles published between 2021 and 2026. The findings identified five themes: AI-mediated language production, cognitive offloading, transformation of linguistic practices, differences in human and AI meaning construction, and linguistic identity transformation. This study highlights that generative AI functions as a cognitive extension while human experience, consciousness, and contextual interpretation remain essential for meaning construction.

documents.abstract: This research synthesizes current empirical evidence on immersive learning approaches through both a meta-analysis of 42 experimental studies (2010-2024) and original data from three case implementations across different educational contexts. Drawing on cognitive science principles including situated cognition, cognitive apprenticeship, and productive failure, the study examines how immersive learning environments create "thick authenticity" by connecting real-world contexts, personal interests, disciplinary practices, and authentic assessment. The analysis addresses the "authenticity dilemma"—balancing complex, authentic challenges with appropriate instructional scaffolding—while critically examining implementation challenges, individual differences that moderate effectiveness, and potential drawbacks. Quantitative results indicate moderate positive effects on knowledge acquisition (g = 0.38, 95% CI [0.31, 0.45]) and stronger effects on transfer (g = 0.61, 95% CI [0.52, 0.70]) and motivation (g = 0.67, 95% CI [0.58, 0.76]), though with significant heterogeneity across designs and implementations. Qualitative data from the case studies reveal that implementation quality, particularly the balance between authenticity and scaffolding, significantly mediates effectiveness. This mixed-methods investigation demonstrates that well-designed immersive learning can develop transferable knowledge, professional identity, and intrinsic motivation, while clarifying boundary conditions and implementation requirements for maximum impact.

The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Using a qualitative conceptual research design, the study synthesizes contemporary scholarly literature, UNESCO and OECD reports, NCERT publications, and Indian educational policy documents published between 2020 and 2026. The thematic analysis identifies five interconnected dimensions influencing inclusive science education: digital equity, virtual laboratories, AI-enabled pedagogy, teacher digital competence, and future-ready science learning. Based on this synthesis, the paper proposes an integrated conceptual framework demonstrating how equitable digital access supports competency-based science education through the interaction of infrastructure, pedagogy, technology, and teacher preparedness. The study argues that meaningful digital inclusion is not merely a technological objective but an educational imperative for achieving scientific literacy, social justice, and equitable learning opportunities in India.

Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning is increasingly used in medical education, including doctor–patient communication training. Such systems may provide virtual dialogue practice, immediate structured feedback, reflection prompts and opportunities for further practice after feedback. However, educational usefulness does not necessarily imply ethical acceptability. This study examined changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions before and after participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway. This longitudinal empirical ethics survey was nested within a course-based randomised educational trial but was analytically independent of the parent trial’s educational outcome analysis. Surveys were administered after random allocation to the AI-supported pathway but before exposure to AI-supported learning functions (T0), at the end of the 8-week course (T1), and at the 3-month follow-up (T2). The main analysis focused on students in the AI-supported pathway with complete T0–T1–T2 ethics-related scale data and analysable T2 open-text responses ( n = 31). The open-text question was included only at T2. The primary comparison was the within-participant T0–T2 change across six ethics-related domains. Two domains showed statistically significant T0–T2 changes. Trust in AI feedback decreased from 3.86 (0.55) to 3.20 (0.62), with a mean change of − 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.88 to − 0.42), Cohen’s d z = − 1.04 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. Room to question AI outputs increased from 2.71 (0.68) to 3.67 (0.58), with a mean change of 0.96 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.23), Cohen’s d z = 1.29 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. The remaining four domains showed small, non-significant changes after Holm–Bonferroni correction. T2 open-text responses indicated that students recognised the formative value of AI feedback while emphasising critical use, teacher supervision, preservation of interpersonal interaction and clearer data governance. This exploratory longitudinal empirical ethics survey showed that, following participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway, two of the six ethics-related domains showed statistically significant changes: trust in AI feedback decreased, while perceived room to question AI outputs increased. These findings support continued attention to ethics-focused evaluation and clear governance arrangements in AI-supported learning pathways.

documents.abstract: The study examines the growing presence of generative artificial intelligence in education and focuses on teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in the teaching and learning process. The development of AI is transforming teaching practices by enabling content personalisation, the creation of educational materials, and more efficient lesson preparation; at the same time, it raises questions about the reliability of generated content, ethical considerations, and teachers' digital competencies. In the context of the specific characteristics of the Polish education system—an ageing workforce, the feminisation of the profession, and the outflow of young teachers—the implementation of technological innovations may be uneven. The study aims to explore teachers’ familiarity with ChatGPT, its use in their daily practice, and the barriers and concerns associated with its adoption. The findings contribute to the discussion on the responsible integration of AI in education and indicate directions for teachers’ professional development.

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a significant influence on various aspects of human life. While there are numerous benefits from utilising AI tools, excessive dependence on them in education raises concerns, especially with regard to youth mental health. This study examines the possible effects of overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on youth mental health. It explores the role of Christian educators in addressing these challenges. The paper provides an overview of mental health by emphasising its multifaceted nature and encompassing emotional, psychological, cognitive, and social well-being. The paper argues that although AI tools have revolutionised education and have led to improvements and productivity, their overuse among young people raises concerns about mental health implications. Such mental health implications include diminished critical thinking, reduced autonomy, impaired memory skills, and social isolation. Moreover, the paper highlights the role of Christian educators in addressing the excessive usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The strategies proposed for combating the concern are AI literacy, curriculum development, mental health awareness, and promoting balanced learning approaches. As Christian educators integrate biblical principles and responsible AI use, the negative effect of AI overdependence among youth will be alleviated.

documents.abstract: Background: Clinical feedback is central to workplace learning in operating room education. While clinical feedback has been conceptualised as relational and context-dependent, less is known about how Operating Room Technology students perceive and experience it within the operating room learning environment. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 17 Operating Room Technology students recruited through maximum variation purposive sampling from Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Data were collected between November 2025 and March 2026 and analysed using Graneheim and Lundman’s inductive content analysis. Trustworthiness was addressed using Lincoln and Guba’s criteria. Results: Five themes comprising 13 subcategories were identified: structural and executive framework of clinical feedback; perceived consequences of clinical feedback quality; harmful feedback practices and barriers; interaction and professionalism in feedback; and individual and professional competencies of instructors in feedback. Students described clinical feedback as most valuable when it was structured, timely, respectful, and dialogic, and perceived it as contributing to confidence, engagement, and professional identity. Delayed, vague, or humiliating clinical feedback was perceived to undermine confidence and psychological safety. Divergent accounts highlighted tensions between immediate intra-operative clinical feedback and workflow demands, as well as circumstances in which public safety-critical corrections were perceived as necessary. Conclusions: The findings suggest that clinical feedback in Operating Room Technology education is a multidimensional process perceived to be shaped by structural, relational, organisational, and educator-related factors. Rather than proposing a new conceptualisation, this study provides a context-specific understanding of how established clinical feedback principles are perceived and negotiated within the operating room learning environment. Strengthening educator capabilities, embedding structured clinical feedback approaches, and fostering psychologically safe learning environments may strengthen clinical education in Operating Room Technology programmes.
